title: Statistics and Machine Learning Assessment
description: 12 questions across 2 sections. Allow 40 minutes. Calculations state their units and rounding; review links identify the relevant lessons. The practice pass mark is 80 percent, not an employer certification.

questions.prompt: Independent observations have population standard deviation 12. With n=36, what is the standard error of the mean, in observation units?
questions.explanation: The standard error is sigma/sqrt(n)=12/6=2 under independence. Dividing by n rather than its square root understates uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A Beta(2,2) prior observes 6 Bernoulli successes and 4 failures. What is posterior mean success probability? Round to 6 places.
questions.explanation: The posterior is Beta(8,6), with mean 8/14=0.571429. The raw sample proportion 0.6 ignores the stated prior.

questions.prompt: For equally likely outcomes x=[1,2,3], what is the population variance? Round to 6 places.
questions.explanation: Mean is 2 and squared deviations sum to 2. Divide by three equally likely outcomes, not the sample-estimator denominator two.

questions.prompt: What does a frequentist 95% confidence procedure guarantee under its assumptions?
options: That every individual observation lies inside the interval
That the model assumptions are true with probability 95%
A 95% posterior probability for every realised interval
Long-run coverage of the fixed parameter by random intervals
questions.explanation: Coverage refers to repeated samples and intervals under the assumed model. A posterior probability requires a Bayesian model; observation coverage is a different target.

questions.prompt: What does a p-value describe under a specified null model?
options: The effect size after all transaction costs are deducted
Probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed
The probability of any future profitable trading strategy
The probability that the null hypothesis itself is true
questions.explanation: A p-value is a tail probability under the null and test definition. It is not the posterior probability of the hypothesis or an estimate of economic effect size.

questions.prompt: Why can dependent MCMC states have low effective sample size?
questions.modelAnswer: Serial correlation means nearby states repeat information, so slow exploration produces fewer independent-equivalent observations.
questions.explanation: Raw chain length ignores dependence. Effective sample size measures information loss from serial correlation and should be read alongside mixing and convergence diagnostics.

questions.prompt: For sum((y-w*x)^2)+5*w^2, no intercept, x=[1,2] and y=[2,4], what coefficient minimises the objective?
questions.explanation: The coefficient is sum(x*y)/(sum(x*x)+5)=10/10=1 for exactly this loss normalisation. A different scaling changes lambda interpretation.

questions.prompt: True values are [1,3] and predictions [2,1]. What is mean squared error, in squared target units?
questions.explanation: Squared errors are 1 and 4; their mean is 2.5. Averaging signed residuals could cancel errors and is not mean squared error.

questions.prompt: Which step belongs inside each training fold?
options: Fit preprocessing globally using validation outcomes too
Use future realised volatility to normalise past labels
Select the final model from repeated final-test inspection
Fit the scaler and feature selector on training rows only
questions.explanation: Learned preprocessing is part of training and must respect each fold boundary. Global fitting and repeated test selection expose the model-selection process to held-out information.

questions.prompt: Which penalty can produce exact zero coefficients?
options: L2 ridge for every finite positive penalty
A shuffled time split regardless of the model
L1 lasso under suitable objective conditions
A larger validation sample without any penalty
questions.explanation: The L1 objective can select zero coefficients because of its kink at zero. Ridge usually shrinks continuously without exact sparsity; validation size does not define a penalty.

questions.prompt: Scalar Kalman predicted variance is 1.1 and measurement variance 0.9 with H=1. What is the gain?
questions.explanation: The gain is 1.1/(1.1+0.9)=0.55. Larger measurement uncertainty would reduce the gain, while larger state uncertainty increases reliance on the observation.

questions.prompt: Why is a smoothed state estimate unsafe as a historical live-trading feature?
questions.modelAnswer: Smoothing uses future observations to revise past states, leaking information that was not available at the historical decision time.
questions.explanation: A filtered state uses information through its timestamp; a smoother can use later data. Good retrospective fit does not make that future information available to a historical strategy.
